title: Who Regulates Online Gambling in Canada in 2026?
excerpt: Canada has no single national gambling regulator. Here is how the Criminal Code, the provinces, Kahnawake and offshore licences actually fit together in 2026.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
If you are trying to work out who regulates online gambling in Canada, the honest answer is that no single body does. There is no federal online gambling regulator and no national register of approved sites. Instead, a constitutional arrangement pushes the job down to thirteen provinces and territories that have each answered the question differently, with a First Nations commission and a long list of offshore licensing bodies at the edges. Understanding that map is the most useful thing a player can do before depositing money anywhere.

Who regulates online gambling in Canada: the Criminal Code sets the frame

Gambling in Canada sits inside criminal law. The Criminal Code makes most gaming and betting unlawful by default, then carves out exceptions. The one that matters most lets a provincial government conduct and manage a lottery scheme within its own borders. That phrase carries real weight: the province is not merely permitting gambling; in law it is the party running the game, even where day-to-day operation is contracted out to private companies.

Two consequences follow. There is no national list of approved sites, because approval is a provincial act. And the rules you play under depend on where you live, not where the operator has its head office. A site fully accountable to a regulator for a player in Toronto may hold no Canadian licence at all in the eyes of an official in Halifax.

Ontario: a regulator and a conduct-and-manage entity

Ontario built the country's first open, competitive online market, and its structure is now the reference point for everyone else. Two bodies share the work. The Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, the AGCO, is the regulator: it registers operators and suppliers, sets standards, audits compliance and enforces. iGaming Ontario is the conduct-and-manage entity, holding the commercial agreement with each private operator so the province remains, in legal terms, the one conducting the game.

Private operators have been able to offer real-money casino games and sports betting to Ontario residents through this framework since April 2022, and the government-run PlayOLG continues alongside the private market. For players, the effect is choice within a supervised perimeter, which is why comparing the casino apps licensed for Ontario players is more meaningful than comparing offers across the open internet.

Alberta: the newest open market

Alberta became the second province to open up. The iGaming Alberta Act, passed in 2025, created the Alberta iGaming Corporation as the conduct-and-manage body, deliberately mirroring the Ontario split, while the Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis commission, AGLC, keeps the regulatory role. The open market launched on 13 July 2026, with the province's PlayAlberta platform continuing in parallel.

Because the Alberta market is only weeks old, things are still settling: the roster of registered operators, advertising practice and the lived experience of the complaints process. Expect the framework to tighten, and treat early marketing claims with the usual scepticism. Our overview of how regulated sports betting works in Alberta covers the launch in more detail.

Everywhere else: the provincial monopoly model

Outside Ontario and Alberta, the model is a government monopoly: the province conducts and manages gaming through a Crown corporation, which runs the only site legally offered to residents.

  • British Columbia is served by the British Columbia Lottery Corporation through PlayNow, which also underpins arrangements elsewhere.
  • Quebec is served by Loto-Quebec through Espacejeux.
  • New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador are served collectively by the Atlantic Lottery Corporation.
  • Manitoba and Saskatchewan reach players through partnership arrangements rather than building platforms from scratch, with Saskatchewan's offering developed jointly with First Nations gaming interests.
  • The northern territories have limited provision, generally routed through lottery arrangements rather than full casino platforms.

Here the regulator and the operator are, in effect, arms of the same government: strong consumer protection and a clear line of accountability, at the cost of variety.

What a Kahnawake licence does and does not mean

The Kahnawake Gaming Commission was established in the 1990s in the Mohawk Territory of Kahnawake, south of Montreal, and has licensed online gambling operators and hosted their servers ever since. It is not a paper regulator: it publishes standards and runs a complaints process that has produced rulings against licensees.

What it does not do is make a site provincially licensed. Its authority rests on Kahnawake's own assertion of jurisdiction, a position never squarely resolved by Canadian courts and one that provincial regulators do not treat as equivalent to their own registration. A Kahnawake licence is better than no licence and gives you somewhere to complain, but it is not the same protection as a site registered with the AGCO or the AGLC.

Offshore licences and the grey area players actually meet

Many sites marketed to Canadians hold licences from Malta, Curacao or the Isle of Man. These are genuine regulators, and Malta and the Isle of Man in particular have long-established rulebooks. Curacao has been overhauling its historically light-touch regime toward a more direct licensing model, which should raise the floor over time.

The critical distinction is what the licence governs. An offshore licence regulates the operator in that jurisdiction; it says nothing about Canadian law and gives no Canadian regulator power to help you. Enforcement in Canada has historically been aimed at operators rather than individual players, but the practical risk sits elsewhere: if an offshore site withholds a withdrawal, your only leverage is a regulator on another continent. That is the grey area, and it is a commercial risk more than a legal one.

How to check a licence yourself

This takes about three minutes and is worth doing every time.

  • Find the licensing statement in the site footer, with the licence number and named corporate entity.
  • Cross-check both on the regulator's own public register rather than trusting a logo, which is trivial to fake.
  • For Ontario, look for AGCO registration and an operating agreement with iGaming Ontario, not one or the other.
  • Confirm the site accepts registrations from your province at sign-up, not just in its marketing.
  • Treat a missing, expired or unverifiable licence as a decision already made for you.

Where complaints and disputes go

In Ontario you raise the issue with the operator first, then escalate to the regulatory and conduct-and-manage bodies, which maintain a route for unresolved player disputes. Alberta follows the same shape through AGLC. In the monopoly provinces you deal with the Crown corporation, with provincial oversight behind it. With a Kahnawake licensee you use the commission's complaints procedure. With an offshore site you go to the operator, then its licensing body, then possibly a dispute resolution service. Each step outward means less leverage.

Advertising rules are part of the answer

Regulation is not only about who holds the money. Ontario restricts inducement advertising, so bonuses, credits and free bets generally cannot be pushed in general-audience media and must instead go through an operator's own channels or to players who have opted in. Standards introduced in 2024 further restricted athletes and celebrities in gambling advertising, barring active athletes outright and allowing retired ones only in responsible gambling messaging. Aggressive bonus advertising aimed at Ontarians in mainstream media is itself a signal about who you are dealing with.

Why the regulator matters more than the bonus

Bonus size is the easiest thing to compare and the least important. The regulator determines whether your funds are segregated, games independently tested, withdrawal terms enforceable, self-exclusion functional, and whether anyone will take your call. That is why our operator reviews and our guide to online casinos in Canada both start with licensing rather than promotions. Work out which framework covers you, verify the licence, then look at the offer.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
